required_facts.statement: Gather information about known risks, blockers, and dependencies while eliciting requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 3: Collect input through the right channels

required_facts.statement: A risk matrix evaluates a risk using its likelihood and impact.
Assess likelihood and impact for each identified risk and use its matrix position to determine a risk level.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/risk-matrix — How to create a risk matrix

text.content: Imagine eliciting requirements for delivery-instruction access. A stakeholder reports that an external address feed may not be ready when needed. Record that known risk together with the blocker or dependency information supplied during elicitation, rather than leaving it outside the requirements discussion.

text.title: Risk Identification in Requirements
text.content: Gather information about known risks, blockers, and dependencies while eliciting requirements.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: A risk matrix evaluates a risk using its likelihood and impact. Assess likelihood and impact for each identified risk and use its matrix position to determine a risk level.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Assess its likelihood and impact. For this hypothetical matrix, the team labels likelihood low, medium, or high and impact low, medium, or high. Suppose the address-feed risk is assessed as medium likelihood and high impact. Place it at that intersection and use the matrix’s agreed risk-level labels to determine its level. The category boundaries are choices for this example; the concept does not supply a universal numerical formula or universal label for that cell.

A second risk might have high likelihood but low impact. Locate it separately rather than assuming frequency and consequence are the same thing. The matrix evaluates both dimensions, so your record should preserve the two assessments as well as the resulting level.

The useful requirements output is a list of identified risks, blockers, and dependencies with reasoned likelihood and impact assessments. It is not a promise that a risk will occur. Nor is merely drawing a grid enough: the assessment and the matrix position must be connected to each identified risk.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Likelihood is not impact. A frequently occurring inconvenience and a less likely severe disruption can occupy different matrix positions. Do not invent a universal score from category words; use the risk-level interpretation of the matrix being used.

practice_anchor.objective: Review a delivery-instruction access requirements list with supplied information about known risks, blockers, and dependencies. For each identified risk, select likelihood and impact, use a supplied matrix to tag the associated requirement with a risk level, and add a one-line rationale.
practice_anchor.success: Each identified risk has separate likelihood and impact assessments, a risk level matching their intersection in the supplied matrix, and a one-line rationale grounded in the supplied information. Requirements without an identified risk are marked as having none identified, rather than assumed risk-free.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make likelihood and impact visible as independent matrix axes with explicit risk-level labels at their intersections. Show the address-feed risk at medium likelihood and high impact, alongside a separate high-likelihood, low-impact risk.

media.group_title: Using likelihood and impact to determine risk level

segments.label: Assess likelihood and impact to place risks on a risk matrix
segments.summary: A hypothetical road-crossing example separates likelihood from impact, called consequence in the explanation. Infrequent bicycles represent low likelihood and low impact; more frequent bicycles increase likelihood without changing impact. Infrequent trucks represent low likelihood but high impact, while frequent trucks represent high likelihood and high impact. A risk matrix places likelihood on one axis and impact on the other, then assigns a risk level at their intersection. In this example, the low–low combination is low risk, the two mixed combinations are medium risk, and the high–high combination is high risk. These levels belong to the illustrated matrix rather than a universal scoring rule.

bridge_note.before: Watch how changing traffic frequency and vehicle type changes two separate assessments. The clip calls impact “consequence”; Devspace uses impact. Its risk-level labels apply to the example matrix.
bridge_note.after: The clip connects likelihood and impact assessments to matrix positions and risk levels. It does not cover gathering known risks, blockers, and dependencies during requirements elicitation; the text supplies that step.

notes: Keep mitigation frameworks and unsupported scoring formulas out of this explanation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Business requirements express the broader business goal or outcome the work should support.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather

required_facts.statement: A requirements document can contain a project summary, goals and success metrics, in-scope and out-of-scope items, requirements, assumptions, and constraints.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Step 4: Document requirements in one shared place

required_facts.statement: Organize the elicited requirements in that shared structure and review them with approvers to agree what will be delivered.

text.content: Suppose the business wants fewer dispatch delays caused by unclear instructions. That broader outcome is a business requirement; it is not yet a detailed description of every action a system must perform.

text.title: Business Requirements Documents
text.content: Business requirements express the broader business goal or outcome the work should support.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: A requirements document can contain a project summary, goals and success metrics, in-scope and out-of-scope items, requirements, assumptions, and constraints. Organize the elicited requirements in that shared structure and review them with approvers to agree what will be delivered.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Organize a shared requirements document around the effort. In this hypothetical document, the summary describes the instruction-access problem, the goal is fewer clarification delays, and a success metric is a stated target for dispatch preparation time. The scope includes the North branch and excludes vehicle purchasing. Record the elicited requirements, along with assumptions such as availability of the current instruction record and constraints such as a required approval. These example entries illustrate the shared structure; they do not prescribe the same content for every initiative.

Review the organized requirements with approvers to agree what will be delivered. If an approver questions the branch boundary or success target, capture the issue rather than treating the document’s existence as agreement. The document gathers the business outcome and supporting delivery context in one place so the review has something specific to consider.

A reader should be able to distinguish the reason for the work from the items expected within its scope. For example, “reduce clarification delays” states the outcome, while the requirement entries describe the agreed needs supporting it. Keep that distinction visible instead of replacing the business goal with a long feature list.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A business requirements document is not made complete by a title or a feature list. The broad outcome and the supporting context need to be clear, and the elicited requirements still need review with approvers. The listed sections are possible contents, not a closed mandatory template.

practice_anchor.objective: Use an editable document template to draft objectives, scope, and a requirements list from a supplied elicitation summary about dispatch instruction access at the North branch. Preserve the business outcome, distinguish in-scope work from exclusions, and flag missing or unresolved information for approver review.
practice_anchor.success: The draft states fewer clarification delays as the business objective, includes the North branch and excludes vehicle purchasing, and organizes the supplied elicited needs into a requirements list without inventing details. Any unresolved target or approval issue is marked for review rather than presented as agreed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show an annotated BRD outline with possible sections for project summary, goals and success metrics, scope inclusions and exclusions, requirements, assumptions, and constraints. Use the hypothetical dispatch example to distinguish the business outcome from supporting requirements, and mark the organized document as ready for approver review rather than automatically agreed.

notes: Preserve “can contain”; keep functional specification detail for its own concept.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Functional requirements state what the deliverable must do.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather

required_facts.statement: Document the expected functions separately from the broader business outcome and from how the solution should perform.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather; Step 4

required_facts.statement: Write a detailed functional specification entry with the initiating event and input values, the expected system response, resulting outputs, and applicable preconditions, postconditions, or exception behavior.

text.content: Imagine the business outcome is fewer dispatch delays. A functional requirement supporting that outcome might be “Display the current delivery instructions when a dispatcher selects an order.” This describes what the deliverable must do, rather than restating the outcome or saying how quickly it should operate.

text.title: Functional Specifications
text.content: Functional requirements state what the deliverable must do.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Document the expected functions separately from the broader business outcome and from how the solution should perform. Write a detailed functional specification entry with the initiating event and input values, the expected system response, resulting outputs, and applicable preconditions, postconditions, or exception behavior.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Expand it into a hypothetical specification entry. The initiating event is selecting an order; the input is the selected order identifier. The expected response is to retrieve and display that order’s current instructions, and the output is the displayed instruction text. A precondition could be that the order exists; a postcondition could be that its current instructions are visible. For an unknown identifier, the example exception behavior is to display a clear not-found result instead of instruction text. These are example requirements, not claims about an existing product.

The detailed entry now gives a reader the behavior for both the ordinary situation and the relevant exception. Keep the broader business outcome in its own place and document performance expectations separately. “Reduce delays” explains why the work matters, but it does not tell the reader what happens when an identifier is selected.

The practical skill is moving from a vague function label such as “instruction access” to an explicit event, inputs, response, outputs, and applicable conditions. Do not invent preconditions or exceptions silently; in real elicitation those details need to be established for the requirement.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A functional specification is not a list of business aspirations. Nor does “fast lookup” fully describe the function. Specify the expected behavior and applicable conditions separately from the broader outcome and the way the solution should perform.

practice_anchor.objective: In a document template, convert the hypothetical BRD requirement to reduce dispatch delays into a functional specification entry for displaying current delivery instructions when a dispatcher selects an order. Use the supplied example details to specify the initiating event, input, expected response, output, precondition, postcondition, and unknown-identifier exception.
practice_anchor.success: The completed entry identifies order selection as the event and the selected order identifier as the input; specifies retrieval and display of current instructions; identifies displayed instruction text as the output; states that the order must exist and that its current instructions become visible; and specifies a clear not-found result for an unknown identifier. The broader outcome remains separate from the function and any performance expectations.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the hypothetical specification structure visible: separate the business outcome from the expected function, and annotate the function with its event, input, response, output, precondition, postcondition, and unknown-identifier exception.

notes: Do not introduce implementation APIs, database commands, or technical design.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A user story describes a desired outcome from a user’s perspective.
Write a story as “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].” to state the user, need, and purpose.
Acceptance criteria describe specific conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be accepted.
Write each acceptance scenario on separate lines using “Given …”, “When …”, and “Then …” in that order.
source_refs: https://cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference/#Example — scenario pattern; Steps; Given; When; Then

required_facts.statement: Given sets the initial context or precondition, When describes the action or event, and Then states an expected result observable to the user or an external system.

text.content: Suppose a dispatcher needs current instructions before releasing an order. An example story is “As a dispatcher, I want to see the current delivery instructions for a selected order, so that I can prepare the correct dispatch.” The persona, need, and purpose are visible without turning the story into a technical design.

text.title: User Stories with Acceptance Criteria
text.content: A user story describes a desired outcome from a user’s perspective.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Write a story as “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].” to state the user, need, and purpose. Acceptance criteria describe specific conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be accepted. Write each acceptance scenario on separate lines using “Given …”, “When …”, and “Then …” in that order. Given sets the initial context or precondition, When describes the action or event, and Then states an expected result observable to the user or an external system.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
The story still needs specific conditions for acceptance. One hypothetical scenario is:
Given an existing order has current delivery instructions
When the dispatcher selects that order
Then the current instructions are displayed for the dispatcher.

Given establishes the initial context, When names the action, and Then states an observable result. Keep the lines in that order. A second scenario could address an unknown order:
Given an order identifier does not exist
When the dispatcher selects that identifier
Then a not-found result is displayed.

These conditions describe what must be satisfied for this story to be accepted in the example. They do not claim the two scenarios cover every need in a real system. Discuss the relevant conditions rather than assuming the story sentence supplies them all.

The BA’s work is to connect the user-perspective outcome with specific acceptance conditions. A reader should be able to see who benefits and then identify the result to check. “The feature works correctly” would not provide the same observable expectation.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: The user-story sentence and acceptance criteria are related but not interchangeable. The sentence communicates the desired user outcome; the scenarios state specific conditions for acceptance. A Then line should describe an observable result, not merely say that the action was performed.

practice_anchor.objective: Convert the hypothetical feature idea of showing a dispatcher the current delivery instructions for a selected order into one user story and two Given-When-Then acceptance scenarios. Address an existing order with current instructions and an order identifier that does not exist.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted written artifact includes a story stating the dispatcher, desired outcome, and purpose. Each of the two scenarios uses separate Given, When, and Then lines in that order, with an initial context, a selection action, and a specific observable result. The scenarios remain consistent with the hypothetical situation.

visual_anchor.purpose: Annotate the dispatcher story to identify persona, need, and purpose, alongside an acceptance scenario whose separate Given, When, and Then lines are labeled initial context, action, and observable result.

notes: Keep stories user-centered; do not introduce later refinement checklists yet.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A use case specifies behavior that provides an observable result of value to an actor or other stakeholder.
An actor represents a role interacting with the subject and may be a person or another system.
Describe a use case’s behavior in natural language with relevant preconditions and postconditions.
Include the basic interaction and relevant variations, exceptional behavior, or error handling.

text.content: Imagine a dispatcher asking an order service for current instructions. In a use case, “dispatcher” is the actor role interacting with the subject; it is not the name of one particular employee. Another system could also act as an actor if it interacts with the subject.

text.title: Use Case Specifications
text.content: A use case specifies behavior that provides an observable result of value to an actor or other stakeholder.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: An actor represents a role interacting with the subject and may be a person or another system. Describe a use case’s behavior in natural language with relevant preconditions and postconditions. Include the basic interaction and relevant variations, exceptional behavior, or error handling.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical use case, state the valued result as obtaining current delivery instructions. Describe the basic interaction in natural language: the dispatcher identifies an order, the service finds its current instructions, and the service presents them. A relevant precondition is that the dispatcher has an order to identify. A postcondition for the successful interaction is that the current instructions have been presented.

Include relevant variations and exceptions. For example, if the identifier is unknown, describe the not-found response. If no instructions are recorded, describe the agreed response for that situation rather than leaving the basic interaction to imply success. The conditions and responses are invented here to show the specification’s structure, not existing tool behavior.

The useful output is an account of behavior that gives an actor or stakeholder an observable result of value, together with the relevant conditions and alternate behavior. A short label such as “view instructions” names an interaction but leaves its behavior unspecified. Conversely, the specification can remain in natural language; this concept does not require programming the interaction.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: An actor is a role, not necessarily a human or a named employee. A use case also needs more than its successful path when variations or error behavior are relevant. Include those behaviors and conditions rather than letting a success-only description stand for every situation.

practice_anchor.objective: Draft a natural-language use case for a dispatcher obtaining current delivery instructions from an order service. Include the actor role, the valued result, a relevant precondition, the main success flow, a successful postcondition, and one alternate flow for an unknown order identifier.
practice_anchor.success: The draft identifies the dispatcher as an actor role and obtaining current delivery instructions as the valued result. It states that the dispatcher has an order to identify, describes the dispatcher identifying the order and the service finding and presenting its instructions, and states that the instructions have been presented on success. An alternate flow describes a not-found response for an unknown identifier. Conditions and responses are treated as hypothetical rather than universal rules.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the hypothetical interaction visible: label the dispatcher actor and order service, show the precondition before the main sequence, show the successful postcondition after instructions are presented, and branch to a not-found response when the order identifier is unknown.

notes: Avoid unsupported use-case templates or UML symbols.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Requirements traceability maintains links from initial business needs through design, development, and testing to the work that fulfills the requirements.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/requirements-traceability-matrix — What is a requirements traceability matrix template?

required_facts.statement: Construct an RTM with a row for each requirement identifier and columns for its originating business need or source, related design artifact, and test-case identifiers; populate these with references to the actual artifacts rather than unlinked descriptions.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/requirements-traceability-matrix — What is a requirements traceability matrix template?; How to get started — 2. Define and categorize requirements for easy traceability; 3. Link requirements to related work items

required_facts.statement: When a requirement changes, follow its links to identify affected work items that need updating.

Review the RTM for missing required links: a requirement without a source link is orphaned from its business justification, and a missing design or test link is a coverage gap when that artifact is required for the stage being reviewed.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/requirements-traceability-matrix — What is a requirements traceability matrix template?; Importance of a requirements traceability matrix template; How to get started — 3. Link requirements to related work items; 5. Track progress with dashboards and reports

text.content: Suppose requirement R-12 says a dispatcher must see current instructions for a selected order. Its originating business need is reducing clarification delays. A traceability matrix keeps that connection alongside links to the work that fulfills and checks the requirement.

text.title: Requirements Traceability
text.content: Requirements traceability maintains links from initial business needs through design, development, and testing to the work that fulfills the requirements.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Construct an RTM with a row for each requirement identifier and columns for its originating business need or source, related design artifact, and test-case identifiers; populate these with references to the actual artifacts rather than unlinked descriptions. When a requirement changes, follow its links to identify affected work items that need updating. Review the RTM for missing required links: a requirement without a source link is orphaned from its business justification, and a missing design or test link is a coverage gap when that artifact is required for the stage being reviewed.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Create a row for R-12 with columns for the originating need or source, related design artifact, and test-case identifiers. In this hypothetical record, link the source to Need-3, the design to Design-7, and the tests to Test-21 and Test-22. These labels stand for actual referenced artifacts in the exercise. A cell saying “some testing” is not the same as a reference to the test artifacts.

Now suppose R-12 changes to include an amended-instruction indicator. Follow its links to identify related design, development, and testing work that may need updating. The matrix helps you find affected work; the requirement change should not remain isolated in its own paragraph.

Review link coverage for the stage being considered. No source link leaves the requirement orphaned from its business justification. A missing design or test link is a coverage gap when that artifact is required at that stage. This qualification matters: do not demand a later-stage artifact merely because its column exists. The practical result is connected requirements and stage-appropriate evidence, not just a table filled with descriptions.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A matrix is not traceability merely because it has columns. Its entries must reference the supporting artifacts. Also distinguish a missing required link from a link to an artifact not yet required at the reviewed stage; the latter qualification should not be discarded.

practice_anchor.objective: Build a five-row RTM for supplied requirements from the hypothetical dispatcher order-instructions situation. Link each requirement identifier to its supplied business source and test-case artifact, and include a related design-artifact column populated where design is required for the reviewed stage. Use artifact references rather than unlinked descriptions; no formulas are needed.
practice_anchor.success: All five requirements have separate rows with references to their actual source and test-case artifacts. Required design links are present. The completed matrix distinguishes missing required links from artifacts not yet required at the reviewed stage.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make requirement-to-artifact links visible in an RTM with requirement, source, design, and test-case columns. Include R-12 linked to Need-3, Design-7, Test-21, and Test-22; contrast it with a row missing its source and a row missing a stage-required test link. Identify linked work for review when R-12 changes.

notes: Do not imply every artifact must exist at every stage.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Requirements documentation needs updating as development and learning change the understanding of the work.
Track the current program status and keep requirements linked to current work-item status.
For a changed requirement, identify and update related work through its traceability links.

Use a customized requirement workflow to distinguish draft (under preparation or review), approved (agreed for delivery), change under review (a proposed revision awaiting a decision), and retired (no longer current); make approval, revision review, and retirement explicit status transitions rather than silently overwriting the current requirement.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/software/jira/templates/document-approval — Workflows; Easy document management; Progress tracking; Customized workflow
atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/itsm/change-management — Change management process — Change request; Change request review; Change approval; Change closure

required_facts.statement: For a proposed change, record the affected requirement and change request, review its risks and expected outcomes, record the approval decision and status, then document the implemented change and its results.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/itsm/change-management — Change management process — Change request; Change request review; Change plan; Change approval; Change implementation; Change closure

required_facts.statement: When the requirement is documented on a Confluence page, modifying that page creates a new version; record the current workflow status in the document, and use More options > Page History to inspect version numbers and compare the revision with the preceding version.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://confluence.atlassian.com/doc/page-history-and-page-comparison-views-139379.html — Access the page history; View the changes made; Compare two versions

optional_enrichment.statement: Preserve the change history when restoring an earlier requirement document: Confluence restoration creates a new current copy of the selected version rather than replacing the historical versions, and lets the user edit the restoration’s change comment.

text.content: Imagine R-12 has been agreed for delivery, then a stakeholder proposes adding an amended-instruction indicator. Requirements life cycle management keeps that revision and its decision visible instead of silently replacing the current requirement.

text.title: Requirements Life Cycle Management
text.content: Requirements documentation needs updating as development and learning change the understanding of the work.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Track the current program status and keep requirements linked to current work-item status. For a changed requirement, identify and update related work through its traceability links. Use a customized requirement workflow to distinguish draft (under preparation or review), approved (agreed for delivery), change under review (a proposed revision awaiting a decision), and retired (no longer current); make approval, revision review, and retirement explicit status transitions rather than silently overwriting the current requirement. For a proposed change, record the affected requirement and change request, review its risks and expected outcomes, record the approval decision and status, then document the implemented change and its results. When the requirement is documented on a Confluence page, modifying that page creates a new version; record the current workflow status in the document, and use More options > Page History to inspect version numbers and compare the revision with the preceding version.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Use an explicit customized workflow. In this example, draft means preparation or review, approved means agreed for delivery, change under review means a proposed revision awaiting a decision, and retired means no longer current. Record R-12’s current status and link it to current work-item status. A proposed revision is not the same as an approved replacement.

Record the affected requirement and change request, review the risks and expected outcomes, and record the approval decision and status. If approved and implemented, document the change and its results. Follow traceability links to identify and update related work. If the requirement is retired, make that transition explicit too rather than leaving an obsolete requirement looking current.

When the requirement lives on a Confluence page, modifying the page creates a new version. Record workflow status in the document, then use More options > Page History to inspect version numbers and compare the revision with the preceding version. Page versions show revisions; the documented workflow status shows whether a revision is draft, agreed, under review, or retired. Keep those two ideas separate.

The BA’s record should let a reader understand the current requirement, the proposed change, the decision, and the resulting work without guessing from whichever paragraph was edited last.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A newer page version does not by itself mean an approved requirement. Approval, revision review, and retirement are explicit workflow transitions. Likewise, editing requirement text without following its traceability links leaves the related work unaddressed.

practice_anchor.objective: Process a sample request to add an amended-instruction indicator to approved requirement R-12 in a simulated Confluence page. Record the request, risks, and expected outcomes; move the customized workflow status to change under review; then apply the supplied approval decision, update linked work, and document the supplied implementation results. Inspect the resulting page versions through More options > Page History and compare the revision with its preceding version.
practice_anchor.success: R-12's record preserves the proposed change and explicit transition from approved to change under review and back to approved following the supplied decision. It records the decision, implemented change, results, and updated traceability-linked work status. Page History retains successive revisions, and the learner compares adjacent versions without treating a newer version as evidence of approval.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make R-12's documented workflow status, change request, decision, and linked work-item status visible alongside its Confluence Page History and an adjacent-version comparison, showing that page revisions and requirement approval are separate records.

notes: Treat workflow as customized, not a built-in universal Confluence status machine.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: Nonfunctional requirements describe how the solution should perform or operate rather than the functions it must provide.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather

required_facts.statement: Make the performance expectation measurable by stating a concrete numerical target rather than a vague request for good performance.
source_refs: atlassian_agile#https://www.atlassian.com/work-management/project-management/requirements-gathering — Types of project requirements to gather — non-functional requirements

text.content: Suppose a requirement says the service must display delivery instructions. That describes a function. A request that the display be “fast” describes a performance expectation, but its wording does not yet supply a measurable target.

text.title: Non-Functional Requirements
text.content: Nonfunctional requirements describe how the solution should perform or operate rather than the functions it must provide.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Make the performance expectation measurable by stating a concrete numerical target rather than a vague request for good performance.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
For this hypothetical situation, stakeholders specify “Current delivery instructions are displayed within two seconds when a dispatcher selects an existing order during normal dispatch preparation.” The numerical target replaces the vague performance word. The function remains displaying instructions; the performance condition says how the solution should perform when doing so.

Compare the two statements side by side. “Display the instructions” answers what the deliverable must do. “Within two seconds under the stated conditions” answers a question about performance or operation. The two-second threshold is example stakeholder input, not a universal definition of acceptable lookup performance.

When documenting the requirement, preserve the concrete target instead of summarizing it back to “good performance.” The measurable expectation gives the requirements discussion something specific to agree about. In this example, a measured three-second display does not satisfy the stated two-second expectation even if a participant describes it as reasonably quick. That is the practical difference between a numerical target and a favorable adjective.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Here, nonfunctional distinguishes how the solution performs or operates from the functions it provides. “User-friendly and fast” is not a concrete numerical performance target. Do not confuse a positive description with a measurable expectation.

practice_anchor.objective: Given the functional requirement 'The service must display delivery instructions for an existing order selected by a dispatcher,' submit three written nonfunctional requirements describing its performance under three clearly stated usage conditions. Give each a concrete numerical target, treating the conditions and targets as hypothetical stakeholder input.
practice_anchor.success: The submitted artifact contains three distinct performance requirements tied to displaying delivery instructions. Each describes how the function performs, includes a numerical target and its applicable condition, and avoids substituting vague adjectives or adding new functions. Example targets are not presented as universal standards.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show 'Display delivery instructions' beside 'Display current delivery instructions within two seconds when a dispatcher selects an existing order during normal dispatch preparation.' Annotate the function, numerical performance target, and applicable condition, and identify the threshold as hypothetical stakeholder input.

notes: Focus on the supported performance distinction; avoid unsupported taxonomies.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

required_facts.statement: A stakeholder is someone interested in the work or someone whose involvement is needed to complete it.
Identify people who use, provide input to, approve, fund, or are affected by the deliverable.
Classify stakeholders as directly involved or affected, indirectly affected or consulted, and reviewers or approvers, noting that roles can overlap.
Record each stakeholder’s role and assess their interest and power over the work.

text.content: Imagine mapping the people involved in changing delivery-instruction access. Dispatch staff use the deliverable; sales staff provide instruction input; an operations manager approves the change; a sponsor funds it. Customer-support staff may be affected by changes in clarification work. These are hypothetical roles, not a fixed stakeholder list for every initiative.

text.title: Stakeholder Identification and Classification
text.content: A stakeholder is someone interested in the work or someone whose involvement is needed to complete it.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Identify people who use, provide input to, approve, fund, or are affected by the deliverable. Classify stakeholders as directly involved or affected, indirectly affected or consulted, and reviewers or approvers, noting that roles can overlap. Record each stakeholder’s role and assess their interest and power over the work.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Record who uses, provides input to, approves, funds, or is affected by the deliverable. Classify their involvement: some are directly involved or affected, some indirectly affected or consulted, and some reviewers or approvers. Roles can overlap. For example, the operations manager might be directly affected by dispatch outcomes and also an approver. Do not force that person into just one category if both roles apply.

Record each stakeholder’s role and assess their interest and power over the work. In this example, a dispatcher may have strong interest in usable instructions but less decision power than the approving manager. The manager’s formal approval role does not tell you everything about their degree of interest, so keep the two assessments visible.

The output is more useful than a contact list: it explains why each person or group belongs in the analysis and how they relate to the deliverable. Begin with involvement and effect rather than assuming only senior people count as stakeholders. People whose work changes can belong even when they do not approve the budget.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: A stakeholder is not only a sponsor or decision-maker. Interest, needed involvement, and being affected can all matter. Classification categories can overlap, so assigning one role should not erase another role the same person actually holds.

Interest and power are recorded separately, with uncertainty noted when the brief provides insufficient evidence.

A finance approver has high power but limited day-to-day interest, while an indirectly affected group has low power and low interest. These are example assessments, not assumptions about everyone with those titles.

text.title: Influence-Interest Matrix
text.content: Plot stakeholders on a grid with separate low-to-high power and interest axes.

text.title: How to apply it
text.content: Manage high-power, high-interest stakeholders closely. Keep high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied. Keep low-power, high-interest stakeholders informed. Monitor low-power, low-interest stakeholders with less intensive engagement.

text.title: A business analysis example
text.content:
Plot them on a grid with a low-to-high power axis and a separate low-to-high interest axis. The manager’s high/high position calls for close management. The high-power, low-interest approver should be kept satisfied. Dispatch staff in the low-power, high-interest position should be kept informed. The low/low group is monitored with less intensive engagement.

Read each position using both axes. Low power does not imply low interest, and high power does not automatically imply high interest. In the example, dispatch staff and the finance approver occupy different quadrants even though both matter to the initiative.

The matrix turns the assessed combination into an engagement approach. It does not identify stakeholders on its own or prescribe a universal message frequency. If you describe the dispatch group as needing information, point back to its assessed low-power/high-interest position rather than simply claiming all users belong there. The practical skill is matching the action to the plotted combination while keeping the assessments explicit.

text.title: Keep the distinction clear
text.content: Do not collapse power and interest into one importance label. “Keep informed” and “keep satisfied” belong to different combinations. A job title alone is not a substitute for assessing and plotting the stakeholder’s power and interest in this work.

media.group_title: Power, interest, and the four engagement approaches

segments.label: Distinguish power from interest and interpret the four quadrants
segments.summary: The Influence-Interest Matrix separates a stakeholder’s power to affect an outcome from their interest in that outcome. Power can come from providing resources, making decisions, or influencing others; interest means how much the stakeholder cares about the result. A stakeholder can be high on one dimension and low on the other. In the construction example, a sponsor may occupy the high-power, high-interest corner, while community members who are not directly affected may occupy the low-power, low-interest quadrant. Each combination suggests a different approach: manage high-power, high-interest stakeholders closely; keep high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied; keep low-power, high-interest stakeholders informed; and monitor low-power, low-interest stakeholders with less intensive engagement.

bridge_note.after: The clip covers both dimensions and all four approaches. Use the text’s instruction-access example to apply the same distinctions; neither stakeholder titles nor quadrant placement prescribe a universal message frequency.
